sentence: They use different methods. What does 'methods' mean here?
setupText: One learner remembers new words with pictures. Another uses short recordings.
taskText: They use different methods. What does 'methods' mean here?
text: One learner remembers new words with pictures. Another uses short recordings. They use different methods. What does 'methods' mean here?
answer: ways of learning
focusKey: coverage-academic-vocabulary-a2-21:Method as how learning is done
explanation: A method is a way of doing something; pictures and recordings are different ways to learn words.

rationales.ways of learning: A method is a way of doing something; pictures and recordings are different ways to learn words.
rationales.reasons for joining: A reason explains why they joined, not how they learn.
rationales.subjects to learn: Both learners are working on words; 'method' describes their approach, not a different subject.
rationales.results of learning: Results come from the activity; the methods are ways of doing it.

sentence: The tutor asks for my source. What should I name?
setupText: For my local-history project, I found the year the bridge opened in a newspaper article.
taskText: The tutor asks for my source. What should I name?
text: For my local-history project, I found the year the bridge opened in a newspaper article. The tutor asks for my source. What should I name?
options: the place where I sat to read
answer: the newspaper article
focusKey: coverage-academic-vocabulary-a2-22:Source as the origin of information
explanation: A source is where information comes from, here the article you read.

rationales.the title of my project: Your project uses the information; it is not where you found it.
rationales.the newspaper article: A source is where information comes from, here the article you read.
rationales.the day I finished writing: That is your work date, not the source of the bridge information.
rationales.the place where I sat to read: Your reading location does not identify the material containing the information.

sentence: Which word describes the second statement as a personal view?
setupText: A course page gives two statements: 'The building opened in 1998' and 'It is the nicest building in town.'
taskText: Which word describes the second statement as a personal view?
text: A course page gives two statements: 'The building opened in 1998' and 'It is the nicest building in town.' Which word describes the second statement as a personal view?
answer: an opinion
focusKey: coverage-academic-vocabulary-a2-23:Opinion as a personal evaluation
explanation: An opinion is a person's view; 'nicest' depends on what someone likes.

rationales.a date: A date tells when something happened; 'nicest' expresses a judgment.
rationales.a measurement: A measurement gives an amount or size, not a personal judgment of beauty.
rationales.an opinion: An opinion is a person's view; 'nicest' depends on what someone likes.
rationales.an instruction: An instruction tells someone what to do; this statement expresses a view.

sentence: What are these notes?
setupText: During a talk, Sam writes 'bus: cheaper; train: faster' to help him remember.
taskText: What are these notes?
text: During a talk, Sam writes 'bus: cheaper; train: faster' to help him remember. What are these notes?
options: the exact words of the whole talk
answer: short pieces of written information
focusKey: coverage-academic-vocabulary-a2-24:Notes as brief learning records
explanation: Notes record useful information briefly, often without full sentences.

rationales.the exact words of the whole talk: Notes can be short reminders; Sam has not written the complete talk.
rationales.questions sent to the speaker: These phrases record information rather than ask the speaker anything.
rationales.marks showing his test result: There is no assessment here; the writing helps Sam remember.
rationales.short pieces of written information: Notes record useful information briefly, often without full sentences.

sentence: What does 'aim' mean here?
setupText: The course aim is to help adults use email. At the start, many learners cannot send a message.
taskText: What does 'aim' mean here?
text: The course aim is to help adults use email. At the start, many learners cannot send a message. What does 'aim' mean here?
options: what the course wants to achieve
answer: what the course wants to achieve
focusKey: coverage-academic-vocabulary-a2-25:Aim versus achieved result
explanation: An aim is an intended result, even before learners have reached it.

rationales.what the course wants to achieve: An aim is an intended result, even before learners have reached it.
rationales.what learners have already achieved: That would be an actual result; an aim says what is intended.
rationales.how long each lesson lasts: Lesson length is a time detail, not the learning aim.
rationales.how much the course costs: The fee is a cost, not what the course hopes learners can do.

sentence: Which part is the definition?
setupText: A dictionary entry says: 'island: land with water all around it'.
taskText: Which part is the definition?
text: A dictionary entry says: 'island: land with water all around it'. Which part is the definition?
options: land with water all around it
the page number of the entry
answer: land with water all around it
focusKey: coverage-academic-vocabulary-a2-26:Definition versus headword and reference details
explanation: A definition explains what a word means; these words explain 'island'.

rationales.island: 'Island' is the word being explained, not its explanation.
rationales.land with water all around it: A definition explains what a word means; these words explain 'island'.
rationales.the name of the dictionary: The dictionary's name identifies the book, not the meaning of 'island'.
rationales.the page number of the entry: A page number helps locate the entry but does not explain the word.

sentence: What is the example doing?
setupText: The tutor says, 'Some courses teach practical skills. For example, this college offers bicycle repair.'
taskText: What is the example doing?
text: The tutor says, 'Some courses teach practical skills. For example, this college offers bicycle repair.' What is the example doing?
options: naming every course at the college
telling learners to repair their bikes
giving one case of a practical course
answer: giving one case of a practical course
focusKey: coverage-academic-vocabulary-a2-27:Example as one case illustrating an idea
explanation: An example is a particular case used to make a general idea clearer.

rationales.naming every course at the college: One course is named; the tutor has not provided the full list.
rationales.explaining why the college opened: The sentence says nothing about the reason the college began.
rationales.giving one case of a practical course: An example is a particular case used to make a general idea clearer.
rationales.telling learners to repair their bikes: Mentioning a course is not an instruction to do the repair now.

sentence: What do we call these blocks of writing?
setupText: Your report has three separate blocks of writing. Each begins on a new line and develops one point.
taskText: What do we call these blocks of writing?
text: Your report has three separate blocks of writing. Each begins on a new line and develops one point. What do we call these blocks of writing?
answer: paragraphs
focusKey: coverage-academic-vocabulary-a2-28:Paragraph as an organized unit of writing
explanation: Paragraphs organize writing into separate units, usually developing a point in one or more sentences.

rationales.headings: Headings name sections; these blocks develop points in the report.
rationales.letters: Letters are individual written symbols, not blocks developing ideas.
rationales.titles: Titles name a whole work or section rather than give the developed explanation.
rationales.paragraphs: Paragraphs organize writing into separate units, usually developing a point in one or more sentences.

sentence: What does 'grade' mean here?
setupText: On this course, written work receives A, B, C or D. My essay received a grade of B.
taskText: What does 'grade' mean here?
text: On this course, written work receives A, B, C or D. My essay received a grade of B. What does 'grade' mean here?
options: my current year level at school
the number of words I wrote
a comment about one spelling error
answer: a rating of my work
focusKey: coverage-academic-vocabulary-a2-29:Grade as a rating rather than a school year
explanation: A grade shows how work was assessed; this course uses letters for its ratings.

rationales.a rating of my work: A grade shows how work was assessed; this course uses letters for its ratings.
rationales.my current year level at school: 'Grade' can refer to a school year in some varieties, but here it rates an essay.
rationales.the number of words I wrote: 'B' is the assessment result, not a word count.
rationales.a comment about one spelling error: A grade is the overall rating here; a detailed comment explains a specific issue.

sentence: These are subjects. What does 'subjects' mean here?
setupText: Marta is choosing between history and computing at college.
taskText: These are subjects. What does 'subjects' mean here?
text: Marta is choosing between history and computing at college. These are subjects. What does 'subjects' mean here?
options: people taking part in a study
pieces of work she must hand in
answer: areas she can study
focusKey: coverage-academic-vocabulary-a2-30:Subject as an area of study
explanation: A subject is an area of knowledge studied on a course, such as history.

rationales.people taking part in a study: 'Subjects' can mean participants, but history and computing are not people.
rationales.areas she can study: A subject is an area of knowledge studied on a course, such as history.
rationales.pieces of work she must hand in: Assignments are pieces of work; subjects are the areas the work concerns.
rationales.rooms where lessons take place: Subjects name what is studied, not the location of teaching.

sentence: Which question does the result answer?
setupText: Learners tested two paper designs. The result was that the folded design held more weight.
taskText: Which question does the result answer?
text: Learners tested two paper designs. The result was that the folded design held more weight. Which question does the result answer?
options: What do we hope will happen?
answer: What happened in the test?
focusKey: coverage-academic-vocabulary-a2-31:Result as an observed outcome
explanation: A result is what an activity or test produced, here the difference in weight held.

rationales.What materials will we need?: That asks about preparation before the test, not its outcome.
rationales.What do we hope will happen?: A hope is an aim or prediction; a result reports what actually happened.
rationales.What happened in the test?: A result is what an activity or test produced, here the difference in weight held.
rationales.Who suggested doing the test?: The originator's identity does not tell us the outcome.

sentence: What does 'research' name here?
setupText: For a project on local shops, we read old records and ask long-time residents questions. Our research takes a month.
taskText: What does 'research' name here?
text: For a project on local shops, we read old records and ask long-time residents questions. Our research takes a month. What does 'research' name here?
options: the work we do to find information
the pictures on our front page
answer: the work we do to find information
focusKey: coverage-academic-vocabulary-a2-32:Research as investigation rather than its presentation
explanation: Research involves investigating a subject to learn more about it, using sources such as records and interviews.

rationales.the final talk we give: A talk may report the research; 'research' names the investigation itself.
rationales.the pictures on our front page: Pictures can be part of a project but are not the whole investigation.
rationales.the marks our tutor gives: Marks assess the work; they are not the work of finding things out.
rationales.the work we do to find information: Research involves investigating a subject to learn more about it, using sources such as records and interviews.

sentence: Why is this a survey rather than a test of their English?
setupText: The college sends learners six questions about their journey to class. It collects the answers in a survey.
taskText: Why is this a survey rather than a test of their English?
text: The college sends learners six questions about their journey to class. It collects the answers in a survey. Why is this a survey rather than a test of their English?
options: It gives a mark for each travel choice.
It teaches learners a new bus route.
It checks whether learners know the timetable.
It collects information about learners' journeys.
answer: It collects information about learners' journeys.
focusKey: coverage-academic-vocabulary-a2-33:Survey versus knowledge test
explanation: A survey gathers information or views; these questions ask about people's travel experiences.

rationales.It collects information about learners': A survey gathers information or views; these questions ask about people's travel experiences.
The journeys are information to collect, not right or wrong answers to score.
A survey asks for information; it is not a lesson explaining a route.
rationales.It checks whether learners know the time: The questions concern their journeys, not knowledge of correct timetable answers.

sentence: What is this way of showing information called?
setupText: The report shows each course's learner numbers with bars of different lengths.
taskText: What is this way of showing information called?
text: The report shows each course's learner numbers with bars of different lengths. What is this way of showing information called?
answer: a chart
focusKey: coverage-academic-vocabulary-a2-34:Chart as a visual display of amounts
explanation: A chart presents information visually; bars can show and compare amounts.

rationales.a timetable: A timetable arranges events by time; these bars compare numbers of learners.
rationales.a chart: A chart presents information visually; bars can show and compare amounts.
rationales.a dictionary: A dictionary explains words rather than compares course numbers with bars.
rationales.a questionnaire: A questionnaire asks questions; this display shows information already collected.

sentence: What does 'total' mean here?
setupText: Four learners came in the morning and six in the afternoon. The total was ten.
taskText: What does 'total' mean here?
text: Four learners came in the morning and six in the afternoon. The total was ten. What does 'total' mean here?
options: the largest of the two groups
the number from both groups together
answer: the number from both groups together
focusKey: coverage-academic-vocabulary-a2-35:Total versus difference or largest amount
explanation: A total is the whole amount after the parts are added together.

rationales.the largest of the two groups: The larger group has six; 'total' combines both groups.
rationales.the number in each group: The groups have different numbers, four and six; ten is not the count in each.
rationales.the number from both groups together: A total is the whole amount after the parts are added together.
rationales.the difference between the groups: The difference is two; 'total' refers to combining, not subtracting.

sentence: Which action matches 'compare'?
setupText: The task says, 'Compare the two college websites.'
taskText: Which action matches 'compare'?
text: The task says, 'Compare the two college websites.' Which action matches 'compare'?
options: Copy the words from one website.
Choose a website without looking at the other.
Find ways the websites are alike or different.
Write instructions for building a website.
answer: Find ways the websites are alike or different.
focusKey: coverage-academic-vocabulary-a2-36:Compare as examining similarities and differences
explanation: 'Compare' means examine things in relation to each other, including similarities and differences.

Copying reproduces text; it does not examine the two sites together.
rationales.Choose a website without looking at the: Comparison requires considering both, not choosing after viewing only one.
rationales.Write instructions for building a websit: That describes a procedure, not similarities or differences between these sites.
rationales.Find ways the websites are alike or diff: 'Compare' means examine things in relation to each other, including similarities and differences.

sentence: What should the summary contain?
setupText: The tutor asks for a summary of a long talk in three sentences.
taskText: What should the summary contain?
text: The tutor asks for a summary of a long talk in three sentences. What should the summary contain?
options: the main points in a short form
the exact words of the whole talk
only your opinion of the speaker
answer: the main points in a short form
focusKey: coverage-academic-vocabulary-a2-37:Summary as brief main content
explanation: A summary gives the important points briefly, leaving out many details.

rationales.the main points in a short form: A summary gives the important points briefly, leaving out many details.
rationales.the exact words of the whole talk: A complete record is not a short summary.
rationales.only your opinion of the speaker: An opinion evaluates the speaker; a summary reports the talk's main content.
rationales.new information on another topic: A summary stays with the original material rather than introduces an unrelated topic.

sentence: What does 'identify' ask you to do?
setupText: A worksheet asks you to identify the capital city named in a short text.
taskText: What does 'identify' ask you to do?
text: A worksheet asks you to identify the capital city named in a short text. What does 'identify' ask you to do?
options: replace it with a different city
find it and say which city it is
decide whether you like the city
answer: find it and say which city it is
focusKey: coverage-academic-vocabulary-a2-38:Identify as recognizing and naming
explanation: 'Identify' means recognize or name the thing requested.

rationales.explain the city's whole history: 'Identify' asks which city it is, not for a full historical explanation.
rationales.find it and say which city it is: 'Identify' means recognize or name the thing requested.
rationales.replace it with a different city: Changing the city is editing the information, not identifying it.
rationales.decide whether you like the city: Personal preference does not identify the city mentioned.

sentence: Which words give the reason for the change?
setupText: The lesson moved online because the college building had no heating.
taskText: Which words give the reason for the change?
text: The lesson moved online because the college building had no heating. Which words give the reason for the change?
options: the college building had no heating
answer: the college building had no heating
focusKey: coverage-academic-vocabulary-a2-39:Reason versus the event it explains
explanation: A reason explains why something happened; the heating problem explains the move.

rationales.The lesson: These words name the event, not why its location changed.
rationales.moved online: This describes the change itself, not the reason for it.
rationales.the college building had no heating: A reason explains why something happened; the heating problem explains the move.
rationales.the college building: Naming the building alone does not explain the problem that caused the change.

sentence: The opening time is a detail. What does 'detail' mean here?
setupText: The article is about a new public garden. It says the gates open at seven each morning.
taskText: The opening time is a detail. What does 'detail' mean here?
text: The article is about a new public garden. It says the gates open at seven each morning. The opening time is a detail. What does 'detail' mean here?
options: the whole subject of the article
the name given to the article
a reason the article was written
answer: one specific piece of information
focusKey: coverage-academic-vocabulary-a2-40:Detail as specific information within a larger account
explanation: A detail is a particular part of a larger account, such as an exact opening time.

rationales.the whole subject of the article: The subject is the garden; the time is one specific part of the information.
rationales.the name given to the article: A title names the article, not a particular opening-time fact.
rationales.a reason the article was written: The opening time does not explain the writer's purpose.
rationales.one specific piece of information: A detail is a particular part of a larger account, such as an exact opening time.
